land.text: the Middle Atlas highlands around Dila, then 'large parts of northern Morocco' conquered from 1637
the Dila'ite lands of central and northern Morocco until 1668, 'when Dila itself was annexed by the 'Alawites after their initial conquest of Fez'

successors.note: The Alawi page: the Dala'iyya capital in the Middle Atlas destroyed in June 1668; Marrakesh taken in July.

capitals.name: Dila (Zawiya of Dila)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Capital: Dila', 'near the qsur of M'ammar, about 10 km southeast of Ait Ishaq' (a second zawiya at Ait Ishaq from 1638). Mohammed al-Hajj was proclaimed Sultan at Fez in 1659 and in 1663 'retreated to the highland capital'. The coordinates are the Saadi dossier's circle for the Middle Atlas base, approximate.

rulers.name: Mohammed al-Hajj
rulers.title: head of the zawiya, Sultan of Morocco 1659-1663
rulers.note: Infobox 'Mohammed al-Hajj, 1637-1668'; the page gives no death date. His family was exiled to Tlemcen after 1668.

correction.text: the Middle Atlas highlands around Dila and Ait Ishaq, the base of the brotherhood

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'From 1637 the brotherhood conquered large parts of northern Morocco' without naming places before 1641; only the highland base is held here. The 70 km circle is the Saadi dossier's reading of the Middle Atlas.

correction.text: the highland base, 'Meknes, Fez and Salé' by 1641 and 'the rest of northern Morocco, including Tétouan', with influence to Ksar el-Kebir and the Taza corridor

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The union is the Saadi dossier's reading of the Dila'iya conquests (Tanger-Tétouan, Taza, Fès-Boulemane, Gharb, Chaouia, Casablanca, Fez, Meknes and Rabat-Salé). Salé is a Dila'iya vassal here (Republic of Salé: 'Under the suzerainty of the Zawiya Dila'iya (1641-1661)') and the page also says 'taken'.

correction.text: the same without Salé, lost in 1661

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'Salé rose against his governor in 1660 and was lost in 1661'.

correction.text: the same without Fez, lost in 1662 'after a putsch led by Qaid Al-Doraidi'; the Dila'ites 'retreated to the highland capital' in 1663

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The page says the Dila'ites ruled 'central and northern Morocco until 1668'; after 1662 Fez is left out and the rest of the north is kept, which the page does not date any further.

region.text: the highland base of the Zawiya of Dila in the Middle Atlas

ledger.note: 1637: the Zawiya of Dila rebels against the Saadis. Infobox 'Rebellion: 1637'; 'From 1637 onwards, the brotherhood started with the conquest of large parts of northern Morocco', under Mohammed al-Hajj. The zawiya itself was founded towards 1566.
1641: the Dila'ites hold Meknes and Fez. 'By 1641 it had taken Meknes, Fez and Salé'; 'In Fez, the Saadi family was expelled and Mohammed al-Hajj was proclaimed Sultan'.

region.text: Salé and Rabat on the Bou Regreg

ledger.note: 1641: Salé submits to the Zawiya. The Republic of Salé page: 'Under the suzerainty of the Zawiya Dila'iya (1641-1661)'; 'In 1641 the Zawiya Dila'iya imposed a religious hegemony over Salé and its parent republic'. The Dila page calls Salé 'taken'.

region.text: the rest of northern Morocco, including Tétouan, the Gharb and the Taza corridor

ledger.note: 1641 (bridge): the rest of northern Morocco. 'It later occupied the rest of northern Morocco, including Tétouan'; 'Its influence extended to Ksar el-Kebir and the Taza corridor'. The page gives no year after 1641, so the conquest is entered at 1641 to match the Saadi dossier's loss.

1659: Mohammed al-Hajj is proclaimed Sultan of Morocco at Fez. 'After the last Saadi sultan died in 1659, Mohammed al-Hajj was proclaimed Sultan of Morocco in Fez'; infobox 'Ruling dynasty of Morocco (1659-1663)'. The zawiya becomes the ruling dynasty of the same state.

region.text: Salé and Rabat on the Bou Regreg

ledger.note: 1661: Salé is lost. 'Salé rose against his governor in 1660 and was lost in 1661' (Republic of Salé: at war with the Zawiya in the early 1660s).
1662: Fez is lost to a putsch. 'Fez was lost in 1662 after a putsch led by Qaid Al-Doraidi.' The regime in Fez surrendered to al-Rashid in June 1666 (Alawi page).

region.text: the Dila'ite lands of central and northern Morocco

ledger.note: June 1668: al-Rashid destroys Dila. 'destroyed their capital in the Middle Atlas in June 1668'; the Dila page: 'Dila itself was annexed by the 'Alawites after their initial conquest of Fez', infobox 'Alawite annexation: 1668'.

wars.name: Dila'iya conquest of northern Morocco
wars.outcome: From 1637 the brotherhood conquered large parts of northern Morocco and by 1641 held Meknes, Fez and Salé; the Saadi family was expelled from Fez and Mohammed al-Hajj proclaimed Sultan.
wars.note: The Alawi page adds that the Dala'iyya invaded the region again in 1646; no page dates a Saadi army defeat in 1638.

wars.name: Fez's revolt of 1651
wars.outcome: 'In 1651, Fez rebelled and invited Muhammad ibn Sharif, but Mohammed al-Hajj forced its submission.'

wars.name: Loss of Salé and Fez
wars.outcome: Salé rose against the Dila'ite governor in 1660 and was lost in 1661; Fez was lost in 1662 after the putsch of Qaid Al-Doraidi; in 1663 Mohammed al-Hajj declined the appeal of Fez's leaders and retreated to the highland capital.

wars.name: Alawite conquest of the Dila'iya
wars.outcome: Al-Rashid 'secured the surrender of Fez in June 1666', 'destroyed their capital in the Middle Atlas in June 1668' and captured Marrakesh in July; the Dila'ite family was exiled to Tlemcen.
wars.note: The Dila page has Dila annexed 'after their initial conquest of Fez'; Salé 'acknowledged his authority' on an undated occasion (Alawi page).

certainty.note: A brotherhood's domain, with towns held and tribes in between: no page gives a frontier.

notes: Cliopatria has no Dila'iya row. The sibling Saadi dossier (af-02-e) records 'dila-iya-sultanate' as counterpart for the 1641 loss of Fez, Meknes and Salé (one event) and of the northern union (another); this dossier uses the same region specs, but draws Salé as a vassal of the Dila'iya (1641-1661, from the Republic of Salé page), whereas the Dila page says Salé was 'taken': the reviewer can fold the Salé circle back into the gain. The Alawi dossier (morocco) records Fez in June 1666 and the Dila capital in June 1668 against 'dila-iya-sultanate'; this dossier has Fez lost to a putsch in 1662 and an autonomous Fez regime surrendering in 1666, so that gain should read 'nobody' or the Fez regime. The Alawi page also dates a Dala'iyya invasion of 1646 (undated outcome). No page opened gives the Dila'ites a presence outside northern and central Morocco, and the Saadi dossier's north union (including Casablanca and Chaouia) is only partly supported ('large parts of northern Morocco'; Tétouan; the Taza corridor; Ksar el-Kebir): it is the researcher's reading shared with the sibling. The rename event marks the 1659 proclamation as Sultan of Morocco at Fez ('ruling dynasty of Morocco 1659-1663'). Gazetteer: all names resolve. After 1668: in 1677 a grandson of Mohammed al-Hajj, Ahmad ibn Abdullah, returned with support from the Turkish regime in Algeria and rallied the Idrassen and other Sanhaja, three government expeditions were defeated before Ismail ibn Sharif overcame the highland forces, and he 'remained in the region until 1680, when he disappeared mysteriously' (Dila page); no land is held, so it is not a war entry. Gaps: no page gives an area, Mohammed al-Hajj's death, or a Dila'ite list of governors.
